Lichen sclerosus (vulva)

An uncontrolled observational study reported improved quality of life after ten PBM sessions, but it could not establish that PBM caused the change or altered disease activity.

Publications and records

1publication

Publication and study types

  • Prospective observational study1

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low certainty for short-term improvement in patient-reported burden (Berthelsen et al. 2024).

Summary of the Evidence

One prospective observational study examined PBM as an addition to existing treatment for vulvar lichen sclerosus. It enrolled 100 women whose symptoms had not been adequately relieved by topical treatment; 94 completed the ten-session course and follow-up. No controlled PBM trial or duplicate report was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

After treatment, seven of eight health-related quality-of-life domains improved significantly. Most DoloTest symptom dimensions also improved, while the smoking-related measure did not reach statistical significance. These are patient-reported changes after a treatment course; the uncontrolled design cannot show that PBM caused them (Berthelsen et al. 2024).

Animal evidence

No animal model study of PBM for vulvar lichen sclerosus was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used an 808-nm near-infrared laser at 500 mW for ten sessions over eight weeks. The first four sessions were planned twice weekly and the remaining six once weekly. The report does not provide a named device model, session duration, or delivered fluence. PBM was used as a supplement to topical treatment.

Interpretation

Most quality-of-life domains improved among women who completed treatment. The result is a favorable change in patient-reported burden during one uncontrolled study; it does not establish that PBM changes the underlying disease or prevents scarring.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

One prospective observational study found improvement in patient-reported quality of life among participants who completed treatment (Berthelsen et al. 2024). Without a comparison group, changes cannot be separated from concurrent topical care or symptom fluctuation, and the study did not establish an effect on objective disease activity, scarring, or long-term symptoms.
